title: Prevention, Scouting and IPM Decision Logic

content.overview: Integrated pest management is a repeatable risk-management system: prevent introduction and establishment, monitor the crop with a defined method, distinguish symptoms from causal evidence, decide whether action is justified, select the least disruptive effective lawful response, and verify the outcome. Strong IPM treats plant health, environment, sanitation, crop history, and organism evidence as one diagnostic system rather than treating every visible symptom as a pesticide problem.

vocabulary.definition: A repeatable inspection and recording process used to detect pests, diseases, damage, and changing crop conditions.
The number or proportion of plants or sampling sites affected by a defined problem.
The degree of damage or symptom expression on affected tissue or plants.
Direct evidence associated with a causal organism, such as insects, eggs, fungal structures, or other identifiable material.
A predefined level of evidence or risk at which an intervention is justified; it is context dependent rather than a universal number.
A prevention-first framework combining monitoring and compatible cultural, physical, biological, and when appropriate lawful chemical controls.

sections.title: IPM begins with exclusion and prevention
sections.body: Clean starting material, quarantine, sanitation, controlled traffic, crop-residue removal, appropriate environmental management, and separation of higher-risk material reduce the probability that pests or pathogens enter or become established. Prevention should be designed into workflow rather than added only after an outbreak.

sections.title: Monitoring must be designed before there is a problem
sections.body: A useful scouting program defines route, sampling locations, tissues examined, frequency, traps or tools used, and the observations that will be recorded. Repeating the same method makes trends interpretable and reduces the bias of only inspecting plants that already look abnormal.

sections.title: Separate symptoms, signs and hypotheses
sections.body: Chlorosis, spotting, wilting, distortion and necrosis are symptoms and can have biological or non-biological causes. Direct organism evidence can strengthen a diagnosis, but distribution, crop history, root-zone data and environmental conditions still matter. Record competing hypotheses before selecting a control when evidence is ambiguous.

sections.title: Spatial and temporal patterns narrow the diagnosis
sections.body: Clustered damage, edge effects, cultivar-specific expression, irrigation-line patterns, propagation-area concentration, or progression across scouting rounds can reveal pathways and rule out alternatives. A close-up photograph without location and time information discards much of this diagnostic evidence.

sections.title: Thresholds connect evidence to action
sections.body: Finding one organism does not automatically justify the strongest treatment. The decision depends on identity confidence, population trend, crop stage, potential rate of spread, tolerance for damage, biological-control compatibility, and applicable regulations. Threshold thinking prevents both delayed response and unnecessary intervention.

sections.title: Use a control hierarchy
sections.body: Correct contributing cultural or environmental conditions where appropriate, physically remove or isolate affected material when practical, preserve or introduce compatible biological controls where justified, and use lawful crop-appropriate chemical controls only within label and jurisdictional requirements. Multiple compatible tactics are often more resilient than repeated dependence on one tactic.

sections.title: Resistance management is part of IPM reasoning
sections.body: Repeated use of the same effective control pressure can select for less-susceptible populations. Where chemical or biological products are used, follow the product label and applicable resistance-management guidance rather than improvising dose, interval, or mixtures.

sections.title: Verification closes the loop
sections.body: After an intervention, repeat the same scouting method and compare incidence, severity, counts, spatial distribution, plant response, and environmental conditions. Improvement supports but does not always prove the original diagnosis; lack of improvement should trigger reassessment rather than automatic escalation.

workedExamples: A few lower leaves show stippling but no organism has been confirmed. Map affected plants, inspect both leaf surfaces with magnification, check traps and neighboring plants, and compare environmental and handling history before choosing a control.

Trap counts rise over three rounds near one doorway while interior counts remain low. The pattern supports investigating entry pathways and strengthening exclusion while confirming organism identity and evaluating whether the trend crosses the facility's action threshold.

A foliar problem stops expanding after airflow and leaf-wetness conditions are corrected. Continue monitoring; the response is evidence that environment contributed, but do not claim a pathogen was identified without organism-level evidence.

A biological control is already established when a new pest treatment is considered. Evaluate compatibility before treatment so solving one problem does not unnecessarily destroy an existing control layer.
commonMistakes: Treating a symptom name as a confirmed causal diagnosis.
Changing several controls at once and losing the ability to interpret the response.
Scouting only visibly damaged plants instead of a representative route.
Using one universal action threshold for every pest, crop stage and production context.
Ignoring biological-control compatibility or resistance-management requirements.
Assuming a product is lawful or crop-appropriate without checking the current label and jurisdiction.
Declaring success immediately after treatment without follow-up measurement.
content.practicalApplication: Build an IPM decision sheet with prevention controls, a fixed scouting route, incidence/severity fields, direct signs, spatial pattern, environmental and root-zone context, competing hypotheses, action threshold, chosen intervention and follow-up date. For a simulated case, document why the evidence supports the selected action and what observation would cause you to revise the diagnosis.
content.summary: IPM is evidence-driven risk management. Prevention lowers introduction risk, structured scouting creates comparable data, diagnosis separates symptoms from causes, thresholds prevent reflexive treatment, compatible controls reduce disruption, and follow-up measurement determines whether the decision actually worked.
